work_order.confidence_rationale: I did not take the proposal on trust: I drove the real makeAsNonChildTransactions with probe fixtures and reproduced findings 1, 2, 4 and 5 exactly as described, then patched the proposed rule in and ran the full loot-core node suite, which gave 1288 passed / 2 failed with the only two failures being the two tests this ticket deliberately reverses — including confirmation that the filled-three-child test still expects 8345 and still passes, which is the load-bearing 'no behaviour change where the old code is right' claim. I also verified both callers, both comment targets, and the Math.abs argument on both arms. Confidence is held below 90 for two reasons: finding 2's correct resolution needs a maintainer's call I do not have (whether the parent or the first selected child should win the category), and the overshoot-in-keep-branch outcome is now pinned to 5345 by arithmetic and a probe rather than by any prior art in the repo. I also corrected one of the proposal's claims — the new badge risk in the keep branch — because my probe showed the function inherits rather than creates the error; had that gone unchecked it would have shipped a wrong statement in the PR description. The proposal's own confidence of 84 was honest and I am two points above it only because I re-verified independently.
work_order.understanding:
PR #81 added a guard to `makeAsNonChildTransactions` that keeps a split parent alive when the rows replacing it are all 0.00, so a never-filled split no longer loses its money (and its schedule occurrence stamp) on unsplit. It implements `every(t => num(t.amount) === 0)` rather than the old work order's sum test, and PR #81 argued at length why: children that OVERSHOOT the parent must still split out, or the surplus the user typed is destroyed. That argument is sound and the two overshooting tests pinning it are correct. The argument does not cover the other side. Every rule that splits out on `=== 0` also splits out when the promoted rows merely FALL SHORT of the parent, and that destroys the parent's amount by the shortfall — 7345 on a 12345 parent with children 5000/0, the whole 12345 on a 5000/-5000 pair. The guard was placed on only one of the two branches in the function: the one that deletes the parent. The neighbouring branch, where two or more children remain and the parent's amount is rewritten as their sum, has no such protection and destroys the parent's amount the same way, one branch below the fix. Three smaller findings round it out: the single-child early return still promotes the parent carrying a stale SplitTransactionError while the newer branch clears it; a test on the surviving row's category asserts the opposite of what the code does and cannot fail on that axis; and two comments describe a rule the code no longer implements.

The council's critic wrote nothing this round (plan/critique.json is `{}`), so there was no critique to judge. Every finding below was therefore reproduced by me directly against the tree, not taken from the proposal on trust: I drove the real `makeAsNonChildTransactions` with probe fixtures for findings 1, 2, 4 and 5, then patched in the proposed rule and ran the whole `loot-core` suite. Five findings hold and are in scope. One (the missing `[AI]` on PR #81's title) is a GitHub action on a merged PR, not a code change. One is bookkeeping about PR #81's work order, which this work order does not repeat. The remaining two are comment restorations.
work_order.root_cause: The guard tests a property of the promoted rows (`all zero`) rather than a relation between the promoted rows and the parent (`do they account for it`), so it fires only on one end of a two-sided condition, and it is placed on one of the two branches that write an amount. In both places the surviving arithmetic is the sum of whatever happens to be there, which silently discards the parent's own value whenever that sum does not equal it.
work_order.approach:
One relation, stated once, applied to both branches.

In the branch that DELETES the parent, replace `promotedRowsAreAllZero` with a test of the relation the guard was always trying to state: the parent may only be deleted when the rows that would replace it account for it. `promotedRowsAccountForParent = !promotedRowsAreAllZero && Math.abs(promotedTotal) >= Math.abs(num(parentTransaction.amount))`, and the guard becomes `if (deleteParentTransaction && !promotedRowsAccountForParent)`. This keeps the all-zero case, keeps the exact-fill case, and — the point — now also keeps the parent when the promoted rows fall SHORT of it, which is the shape the ticket exists for. It deliberately does NOT fire on overshoot, so PR #81's two overshooting tests and its stated reasoning survive unchanged. The comparison is on absolute values, not signed ones: a plain `promotedTotal >= parentAmount` reads `-5000 >= -12345` as true for an under-filled expense, so a 123.45 expense split into -50.00 and 0.00 would still be destroyed. `Math.abs` is load-bearing for negatives and I verified both arms of it by probe.

In the branch that KEEPS the parent, stop recomputing its amount as the sum of the remaining children. The parent's amount after an unsplit is its own amount less what left, which is `num(parentTransaction.amount) - promotedTotal`. For a correctly filled split this is identical to the sum of the remaining children — I verified `12345 - 4000 = 8345`, and the existing test expects `8345` — so the existing filled-three-child test passes untouched. For an unfilled one it is the difference between destroying the parent's amount and preserving it: 12345 with children 5000/4000/0 and one leg unsplit goes to 7345 (conserved: 7345 + 5000 promoted = 12345) instead of 4000, and 12345 with three 0.00 children goes to 12345 instead of 0.

Also: give the single-child early return `error: null` so both branches producing the same surviving row agree, and fix the category test so it can fail on the axis it claims.

On the category finding I am fixing the TEST, not the behaviour. `makeTransactionWithChildCategory` takes the category off the promoted row, and the test at :507 gives parent and both children the same category, so it passes whatever the implementation does while its comment and name assert the opposite. Child-category-wins is established, deliberate behaviour elsewhere in the same file — the single-child test at :398 pins exactly that — so the two-child branch agreeing with it is consistent, not a bug. The test gets three distinct categories, the real provenance asserted, and a name that says which category lands. Whether the parent SHOULD win is a maintainer's call, recorded in risks rather than silently taken.

One correction to the proposal, from my own probes: it claims the new keep-branch rule introduces a fresh `SplitTransactionError` on an overshoot. It does not. `makeAsNonChildTransactions` never creates a split error — it spreads `...parentTransaction` and so passes the parent's EXISTING error through untouched on both the old and the new code. I verified this by running the overshoot shape against original and patched code: old gives `p:7000` with the error, new gives `p:5345` with the same error. The difference is that the OLD amount (7000) happened to equal the sum of the remaining children, leaving a stale badge on a now-balanced split, while the NEW amount (5345) does not, which is the arithmetically honest outcome. So the badge is inherited in both cases and the new rule does not add one. Do not treat this as a new risk in the PR description; it is an improvement, and the underlying staleness is a separate pre-existing gap noted in residual_risks.
work_order.debate_summary:
There was no debate to arbitrate: plan/critique.json is `{}`, so the critic produced nothing this round. Rather than treat an empty critique as a clean bill of health, I re-verified the proposal myself against the code, and that was worth doing — it caught one wrong claim.

What I confirmed. All four behavioural findings reproduce exactly as the proposal described, driven through the real function rather than by reading it: the 7345 destroyed on 5000/0, the whole 12345 destroyed on 5000/-5000, the parent surviving at 0 on three-zero children, the 2945 destroyed on 5000/4000/0, the category coming from the first SELECTED child, and the single-child return keeping its SplitTransactionError. I patched the proposed rule into the tree and ran the full loot-core node suite: 1288 passed, 2 failed, and the only two failures are precisely the two tests this ticket says are wrong. The proposal's evidence and its confidence of 84 were honest and load-bearing.

What I corrected. The proposal lists as a residual risk that an overshoot in the keep-parent branch 'now leaves a SplitTransactionError on the remaining split where the old code balanced it'. I ran that exact shape against both versions of the function and it is not what happens. `makeAsNonChildTransactions` spreads `...parentTransaction` and never calls `recalculateSplit`, so it does not create split errors — it passes the parent's existing one through. Original code: p=7000 with the inherited error. Patched code: p=5345 with the same error. The badge appears in both cases; what differs is that the OLD amount happened to equal the sum of the remaining children, leaving a stale badge on a balanced split, whereas the new amount is the arithmetically honest one. So the risk as written is not merely overstated, it is inverted, and shipping it would have put a false statement in the PR description. I dropped it from risks and moved the underlying, genuinely pre-existing gap — a parent whose amount changes without its error being recomputed — to out_of_scope with a reason, since fixing it means touching error handling and would widen a defect-shaped change.

Where I sided against the proposal. Two places. First, I kept both overshoot cases as tests to preserve, but I explicitly told the implementer not to assert a SplitTransactionError in the new multi-remaining overshoot case, because the function never mints one — the proposal's test list would have had someone write a failing assertion. Second, I added AC-7 (zero-amount parent keeps its schedule stamp) as its own criterion, which the proposal folded into evidence rather than acceptance; that arm is the one the original guard existed for and the rewrite must not regress it, so it deserves to be checked rather than assumed.

What I did not overturn. The proposal's judgement call on finding 2 — fix the test, not the behaviour — is right, and I verified the thing that justifies it: the single-child test at :398 already pins child-category-wins as deliberate, so the two-child branch agreeing is consistency rather than a bug. Whether the parent should win is a maintainer's call, recorded in risks rather than taken silently. I also agree with dropping findings 3 and 8 (a merged PR's title, and bookkeeping about a past work order), with the two comment restorations, and with every rejection in alternatives_considered — I re-derived the `Math.abs` argument independently and it holds.

One thing the council did not examine and I could not settle: the rewrite's effect on how the register renders a kept-but-unbalanced parent. I traced the badge path far enough to know the function does not recompute the error, but I did not read TransactionsTable.tsx:2339 or run the app. That is in unknowns and is the first place QA should look.

assumptions: `nonChildTransactionsToUpdate` is the complete set of rows that will exist after the unsplit whenever `deleteParentTransaction` is true — i.e. the selected children plus the one remaining child appended at :468-474. The probes exercise both shapes and both behave as the rule predicts, but I have not proved the partition by exhaustion; a caller passing an id set that is neither the children nor the parent would break the invariant.

The parent row's `amount` is authoritative for the parent's money and the children's amounts are the user's allocation of it. Every rule here follows from that: a shortfall belongs to the parent, and a surplus cannot. If the product intends the reverse for under-filled splits, AC-2 and the two flipped tests are the wrong answer and the approach needs revisiting rather than adjusting.

`Math.abs` on the comparison is right rather than a signed comparison with an explicit sign check. Arithmetic supports it and both probe arms confirm it, but no shipped test covers expenses through this function, so this rests on reasoning and probe rather than prior art in the repo.

Nothing downstream depends on the parent's amount being the sum of the remaining children. I grepped every caller; both build `transactions-batch-update` diffs and neither the client handler nor `batchUpdateTransactions` recomputes or reconciles a split total from the parent's amount.

Clearing `error` to `null` on the single-child early return cannot hide a real problem. The row it produces is a plain transaction with no children, for which a split error is meaningless by construction — and RepairTransactions.tsx already exists to sweep non-split rows carrying split errors.

The demo budget from 'View demo' contains both income and expense transactions large enough to split, so the expense cases in AC-6 and the qa_script are reachable without hand-building a budget. Not verified by running the app — I did not launch it.
unknowns: Whether the parent or the child SHOULD win the category on the surviving row. The test is fixed to pin current behaviour and the code is unchanged; a maintainer may want the opposite, which is a one-token change at :506 plus the flipped test. Recorded in risks.

Whether the reviewer's intent on finding 4 was the narrow all-zero test or the general relation. The general relation was chosen because it is identical on every filled split and correct on every unfilled one, but a reviewer reading it as scope creep is not misreading it.

Whether `error: null` on the single-child return is reachable through any UI gesture. Neither the review nor I could construct it through `deleteTransaction`; it is fixed because the two paths produce the same row and disagree, which is a consistency defect whether or not a user can currently reach it.

How the register renders a parent whose children no longer sum to its amount after the keep-branch rewrite. The badge path is TransactionsTable.tsx:2339 and the mobile editor is TransactionEdit.tsx:306; neither was read in detail and the app was not run, so the visual consequence of a kept-but-unbalanced parent is unverified.

Whether any e2e test in packages/desktop-client/e2e covers unsplitting. A grep for 'unsplit' across that directory found nothing, so the function appears to be covered only by unit tests — which means AC-1 through AC-6 are browser-verified for the first time.
residual_risks: The keep-parent rewrite deliberately leaves the parent's amount not equal to the sum of its remaining children whenever the split was under- or over-filled. The money is conserved, but the parent is now an unbalanced split, and nothing in this path recomputes its error. QA should look here first: unsplit one leg of a partly-typed three-leg split and check what the register renders on the parent — a red unassigned-amount badge is the arithmetically honest outcome, but it is new on screen and nobody has looked at it.

The surviving row's category comes from the first SELECTED child, so it depends on selection order. A user who categorizes one leg of a partly typed split and then unsplits loses the parent's category to that leg's. Unchanged behaviour that the old test hid; the new test pins it. NOT fixed here — that is a behaviour change needing a maintainer's call.

Under-filling a split and unsplitting it now discards the amounts the user typed into the children. This is the ticket's explicit instruction and PR #81 shipped the opposite, so two shipped tests flip. Anyone who liked the old behaviour will read this as a regression; it is the intended correction, and the PR description should say so plainly rather than letting QA discover it.

The negative-amount (expense) arm is pinned only by tests written in this change. No shipped test covered expenses through this function, so if `Math.abs` is later 'simplified' away, the new tests are the only thing standing between that and a regression.

Findings 8 and 9 of the review were accepted in part only. The comment trim for finding 9 is done; the structural suggestion (hook pair plus a construction-only helper) is not, and the review's own first option goes unaddressed. If a reviewer re-raises it, the answer is that it was considered and traded for blast radius — that reasoning is in alternatives_considered and should be repeated in the PR description.

PR #81's title still lacks the `[AI]` prefix and this diff does not fix it — it is a merged PR. The prefix requirement is carried onto this ticket's own PR via the qa_script instead, so QA must actually check it; it is exactly the kind of step that gets skipped.

AC-1 through AC-6 are browser-verified for the first time — no e2e test covers unsplitting. If the demo budget lacks a splittable expense, AC-6 cannot be checked as written and needs a hand-built one.
